title: Al-Hajjaj and the Pious Man

full_text:
Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the formidable governor of Iraq, was notorious throughout the Islamic empire for his unbending severity, his swift execution of political rebels, and his terrifying temper.

One afternoon, a venerable and pious scholar named Said ibn Jubayr was brought before his tribunal in chains, accused of speaking against the governor’s harsh exactions upon the peasantry.

Al-Hajjaj glared at the prisoner with eyes like burning coals: 'Tell me, old man: what think you of my governance?'

Said replied with tranquil composure: 'You have built cities, O Hajjaj, but you have neglected justice; you have enforced order with fear, but you have dried up the fountain of mercy.'

Al-Hajjaj struck his armrest: 'Do you not fear that a single word from my lips can order your head struck from your shoulders this very minute?'

Said smiled with serene fearlessness: 'If my life were in your hands, O Hajjaj, I would have trembled before you. But my life and death reside entirely in the hands of the Creator of the heavens, without whose decree not a leaf falls from the tree. You can only destroy a frail earthen vessel; my spirit and my truth are beyond your reach.'

Al-Hajjaj was shaken to his core by the prisoner’s absolute absence of fear. For the first time in his life, the fierce governor found his authority powerless against a man who possessed no worldly attachments.

Al-Hajjaj lowered his eyes, ordered the chains struck from Said’s wrists, and said quietly: 'Depart in peace, O Said! By heavens, your faith is an iron fortress that makes all my armies look like children playing with straw.'
moral: Spiritual integrity and moral courage disarm the fiercest tyranny, commanding respect from oppressors.
